opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, and I want to be careful, because the FDA exists for real reasons. Thalidomide happened. There's a reason we have a system that's cautious about putting things into people's bodies. So I'm not someone who says "just tear it all down." But I do think the current system was designed for a world where drug discovery is slow, expensive, and mostly trial-and-error, and if AI changes that, the bottleneck shifts almost entirely to the clinical and regulatory side.

A few things I'd think about. First, the clinical trial process itself. A lot of the time and cost isn't the regulator saying no; it's that trials are slow to enroll, poorly designed, and run sequentially when they could be adaptive. AI can help design better trials, identify the right patient populations, predict who's going to respond, and pick biomarkers that tell you much earlier whether something is working. So part of the change is the FDA being more open to adaptive designs, surrogate endpoints that are actually well-validated, and smaller, smarter trials when the mechanistic evidence is strong.

Second, I think there's an asymmetry in how we count harms. When a drug that causes harm gets approved, that's very visible, there are hearings, people get blamed. When a good drug is delayed by five years, the people who died in those five years are statistical, invisible. Nobody holds a hearing for them. If AI really does compress, say, fifty or a hundred years of biological progress into five or ten, then the cost of delay goes way up, because each year of delay is withholding a lot more value than it used to. The regulatory system should internalize that.

Third, and this is more speculative, if we get to the point where AI models of biology are genuinely predictive, where you can simulate toxicity or efficacy with real confidence, then you could imagine some of that in-silico evidence counting toward approval, the way animal models count now. We're not there yet, and I'd want that validated very rigorously before anyone leans on it. But I think the regulators should be building the capacity now to evaluate that kind of evidence, rather than waiting until it's here and then spending a decade figuring out what to do with it.

And honestly, the agencies themselves could use AI. A lot of review is reading enormous dossiers, checking data, cross-referencing. That could get dramatically faster without lowering the bar at all.

So the summary is: I'd keep the safety standard, but I'd make the process much faster and much more evidence-flexible, and I'd make sure we're weighing the cost of delay as seriously as the cost of error. Because if the science moves at AI speed and the approvals move at 1990s speed, we'll have left most of the benefit on the table.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could compress decades of biological progress into years and that clinical and regulatory processes would become the bottleneck, with approvals lagging behind AI-speed science.

r002.rationale: It supports faster, more flexible review when mechanistic evidence is strong, but does not argue that requirements built for marginally effective drugs with serious side effects are excessive for drugs with clearly established safety and efficacy.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most important questions, because my view is that the science is going to move much faster than the institutions around it, and if we're not careful the institutions become the bottleneck. In the essay I wrote, I talked about this idea of a "compressed 21st century," where we get something like fifty to a hundred years of biological progress in five or ten years. And one of the things I said is that the limiting factor won't be the discovery part, it'll be the clinical trial part, the regulatory part, the deployment part.

So let me say a few things. First, I want to be careful here. I'm not one of these people who thinks the FDA is just a bunch of bureaucrats who should get out of the way. The FDA exists for a reason. Thalidomide happened. There are real harms from drugs that don't work or that hurt people, and a lot of the regulation is written in blood. So I don't want to start from "deregulate everything."

But I think the key insight is that the current system is designed around a particular set of assumptions about how much we know. Phase one, phase two, phase three, these are essentially a way of being empirical because we don't have a good enough model of the underlying biology to predict what's going to happen. We dose a few people, then more people, then a lot of people, because we don't know. If AI changes the amount we know, then the right structure of the regulatory process should change too, and I think it should change in a few directions.

One is on the trial design side. If you have AI systems that can model pharmacokinetics, model toxicity, model which patient subpopulations will respond, you should be able to run smaller, faster, more targeted trials and get the same statistical confidence. Maybe better. The FDA actually has some flexibility here already, things like adaptive trial designs, but they're used cautiously. I think the regulator should be much more willing to accept trials where the design was informed by predictive models, as long as you can validate the models.

Two, and this is maybe the more radical thing, I think we need to think about the endpoint of regulation as something like a probabilistic risk-benefit assessment, rather than this fixed sequence of hurdles. If an AI system can say, with a degree of confidence we can check against reality, that this molecule is very likely safe and very likely effective for this population, then the question should be, "how good is this prediction, and how do we calibrate it," not "did you check these seven boxes."

Three, I think there's an underrated thing around the speed of the agency itself. A lot of the delay isn't the trials, it's the review. It's the back and forth. And that's a place where AI could just make the regulator faster, if the regulator is allowed to use it. I'd love to see the FDA be an early adopter rather than a late one.

And then the last thing I'd say is that there's a bit of a chicken and egg problem. Regulators are reasonably going to say, "show me that these models actually work before I rely on them." And that's fair. So I think there should be a deliberate process, maybe a sandbox or a pilot track, where AI-informed approaches run in parallel with the conventional process, and we accumulate the evidence that they're as good or better. Then you expand. You don't flip the switch all at once.

I'll also just be honest that I think the bigger risk right now isn't that regulators are too permissive about AI. It's that the political and institutional timeline is just slow by default, and if we really do get the kind of acceleration I think is possible, millions of people could be waiting for things that already exist. That's the scenario I worry about. So I'd want the conversation to start now, before the capabilities are fully here, rather than after.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that biological progress will accelerate dramatically and says clinical trials, regulation, and deployment will become the limiting bottlenecks.

r002.rationale: The response supports changing fixed approval hurdles when AI can predict safety and efficacy, but does not say those requirements were designed for drugs with marginal efficacy and serious side effects.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking what becomes the bottleneck if AI makes the discovery of new treatments much faster. You could have a world where we’re very good at designing drugs, but it still takes many years to find out whether they work and get them to patients. In that world, accelerating discovery only gets you part of the benefit.

I wouldn’t take that to mean we should just approve whatever an AI says is safe. The prediction and the evidence are different things. But I would want a system that’s much better at running trials quickly, learning from the results as they come in, and adjusting the trial accordingly. You should be able to stop an ineffective treatment earlier and expand a promising one faster.

There’s also a question about how we weigh risk. If someone has a fatal disease and no effective treatment, waiting is itself a risk. We should account for that explicitly, alongside the risk of approving something that turns out not to work or has serious side effects.

Over time, if AI models demonstrate that they can reliably predict particular kinds of toxicity or treatment outcomes, that evidence should change what testing we require. But you have to establish that reliability empirically. You can’t assume it just because the model is impressive in other domains.

So the direction I’d favor is faster, more adaptive, more evidence-driven approval, with much better follow-up after approval. The goal is to shorten the time it takes to learn whether a treatment helps people.

r001.rationale: It says faster discovery could leave trials and patient access as bottlenecks, but does not predict that drug discovery will overwhelm the approval pipeline’s capacity.

r002.rationale: It supports faster, adaptive approval and changing testing requirements when AI predictions are empirically reliable, but does not argue that requirements for drugs with clear safety and efficacy may be excessive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central question is whether the process can handle a world where we’re discovering effective treatments much faster. If AI greatly increases the rate at which we generate promising drugs, but the capacity to test them stays fixed, then clinical trials become the bottleneck.

I wouldn’t respond by saying, “Let’s just approve everything.” You still need to know whether a treatment works and whether it’s safe. But I’d want a much more adaptive process, where you can learn from results as they come in, stop unsuccessful trials earlier, and expand the promising ones. And I’d want the evidence requirements to reflect the circumstances. Someone with a terminal disease and no effective treatment faces a very different decision from a healthy person considering a preventive drug.

There’s also a distinction between using AI to generate a hypothesis and using it to establish that the hypothesis is true. A model saying a drug should work isn’t enough. Over time, if its predictions are validated against actual outcomes, perhaps that evidence can help us design smaller, faster, more informative trials.

So I’d focus on making the system better at learning. The goal is to reduce the time it takes to find out what actually helps people, while preserving the checks that make those conclusions trustworthy.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AI may generate promising drugs faster while testing capacity stays fixed, making clinical trials the bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It discusses tailoring evidence requirements to patient circumstances and validated predictions, but does not argue that requirements for drugs with clear safety and efficacy are excessive.
